bull_bear.body: - Net debt INR 749 cr (incl. term + working capital) at end-9MFY26. Leverage temporarily up from inventory pre-securing; mgmt stresses "capital discipline" and "disciplined growth over aggressive volume." No dividend/buyback discussion.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- Commodity volatility (silver ~9% daily swings) compressing spot-order margins.
- Industry overcapacity: ~140 GW ALMM module capacity, cell capacity 26 GW (12 GW obsolete Mono PERC) heading to 50-60 GW — mgmt downplays (industry util only 40-50%).
- Execution risk on Odisha cell ramp/efficiency stabilization. Rising interest cost. US tariff/policy uncertainty (final terms unsigned). Demand timing tied to ALMM cell mandate (tenders from ~June 2026, 18-24 month lag to installation).
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: - Confident, execution-focused; candid on margin dip drivers and partial pass-through; refused to disclose absolute realizations/market prices (typical). Emphasized 10-yr track record and disciplined growth. Some defensiveness/circularity in the flat-volume QoQ exchange. Credible on funding (fully tied up).
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The real margin re-rating is cell/DCR-led from H2FY27, not module volume — module pricing is a commodity pass-through game.
- Interest-cost spike is a deliberate strategic inventory bet on rising cell/silver prices, not distress — watch if it actually normalizes by March.
- Q4→Q1FY27 volume explicitly flagged flattish; new 4 GW module won't be fully available in FY27 (ramp). Mono PERC obsolescence is a tailwind for new cell capacity vs incumbents.
- Solar pump BU and inverter assembly are early call-options, immaterial today.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- One of the largest single-location solar module manufacturing hubs in India, with three fully automated plants at Ambala aggregating 4.8 GW
- Backward integration into EPE encapsulant film, in-house solar cells and planned ingots and wafers, reducing dependence on imported cells that are currently the primary cost input
- Integrated single-point offering combining in-house module manufacturing with EPC and O&M project execution
- Early adoption of Mono PERC and n-Type TOPCon technology, enabling response to evolving efficiency and reliability requirements
- Confirmed order book of approximately 5.89 GW as on March 31, 2026, balanced across utility-scale, C&I and government projects, mitigating customer concentration risk
- Export access to tightly regulated markets: manufacturing to a fully traceable Bill of Materials with compliance to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act and Non-Foreign Entity of Concern requirements
- Strengthened credit profile post the September 2025 IPO, with CRISIL upgrading long-term bank facilities to CRISIL A-/Stable and assigning CRISIL A2+ to short-term facilities
- Distribution reach through 81+ channel partners across India and a US subsidiary serving the North American market
- Track record of over 6 GW of modules supplied since inception across domestic and international markets
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on imported solar cells as the primary cost input — The MD&A states that the upcoming Odisha cell capacity will materially reduce dependency on imported cells, described as currently the primary cost input, and that in-house EPE film production reduces dependency on external suppliers, primarily Chinese imports. Until Odisha ramps, procurement remains exposed to external supply and pricing.
- Margin compression from industry-wide pricing normalisation and elevated input costs — Management attributes the moderation of EBITDA and PAT margins during FY 2025-26 primarily to industry-wide pricing normalisation, elevated solar cell procurement costs, and higher operating expenses associated with capacity expansion.
- Execution and ramp-up risk on the Odisha greenfield integrated project — A large share of planned capacity - 4 GW of modules, 2.4 GW of Phase I cells with 3.6 GW in Phase II, and 6 GW of planned ingots and wafers - is still under ramp-up or planning, with an ALMM-II inspection due in September 2026 and ingot/wafer commissioning only targeted by FY29. Realisation of the 8.8 GW module footprint depends on delivering these phases.
- Single-site operating concentration during the year — The Ambala facility was explicitly the Company's only operating facility during FY 2025-26, so production, at 84.07% utilisation against 4.8 GW of installed module capacity, was concentrated in one location until Odisha commissions.
- Regulatory and policy dependence on the ALMM and duty regime — Demand and competitive position are tied to policy: ALMM List-II for cells becomes mandatory from June 01, 2026 and ALMM List-III for wafers from 1 June 2028, while the BCD and AIDC tariff regime (40% on modules, 25% on cells plus surcharges) is what protects domestic manufacturers from Chinese dumping. Government schemes such as CPSU Phase-II, PM-KUSUM and PM Surya Ghar are named demand drivers.
- Rapid industry capacity build-out and competitive intensity — India's module manufacturing capacity expanded to over 120 GW by March 2026 from around 38 GW in March 2024, with ALMM List-I crossing 100 GW across more than 100 manufacturers, while cell capacity reached approximately 27 GW. This scale of supply addition is a structural pricing risk for module manufacturers.
- Capital intensity and funding of the expansion programme — Management notes a meaningful share of capital is deployed in manufacturing assets yet to commence commercial production, plans approximately INR 17,000 million of investment in FY 2026-27 funded through a balanced mix of internal accruals and debt, and had deployed only about 56% of IPO proceeds as of March 31, 2026 - so returns depend on commissioning and utilisation rising.
- Customer concentration in the order book — The MD&A explicitly frames the balanced mix of utility-scale, C&I and government projects within the approximately 5.89 GW confirmed order book as supporting business stability while mitigating customer concentration risk, identifying concentration as the underlying exposure.
- Export market compliance requirements — Access to tightly regulated solar markets depends on manufacturing to a fully traceable Bill of Materials and complying with the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act and Non-Foreign Entity of Concern requirements; these are stated as key regulatory conditions for market access.
- Execution risk from rapid diversification into adjacent businesses — Within a single year the Group entered transformers (80% of Melcon), battery energy storage (SPSSL, incorporated March 2026), power electronics (UDAY inverters) and independent power production (49% of IHSPL with a 41 MW AC PPA), each a new capability requiring its own processes, talent and quality systems.

outlook.body: Saatvik is executing a phased capacity expansion built around backward integration. The flagship Odisha Greenfield Integrated Manufacturing Project at Gopalpur, spearheaded by wholly owned subsidiary Saatvik Solar Industries Private Limited, saw civil and structural works across the solar cells and modules units substantially completed during FY 2025-26. Phase I comprises 2.4 GW of solar cell capacity and 4 GW of module capacity, both under ramp-up, with the ALMM-II inspection planned for September 2026; Phase II is planned to add a further 3.6 GW of solar cells, taking planned Odisha cell capacity to 6 GW (raised during the year from 4.8 GW). A further 6 GW of ingot and wafer capacity is planned, with commissioning targeted by FY29. On completion, total module manufacturing capacity is expected to rise from 4.8 GW at Ambala to 8.8 GW across Haryana and Odisha. At Ambala the Company commissioned a 2 GW EPE encapsulant film facility during the year and plans to enhance encapsulant capacity to 5 GW across Ambala and Odisha (Odisha encapsulant of 2 GW is planned). Management plans to invest approximately INR 17,000 million in FY 2026-27, primarily in the Odisha project, funded through a balanced mix of internal accruals and debt while remaining within the targeted gearing range; approximately 56% of IPO proceeds had been deployed towards manufacturing expansion, backward integration and debt reduction as of March 31, 2026. Expansion also came inorganically: an 80% equity stake in Melcon Transformers and Electricals Private Limited (Alwar, Rajasthan plant, transformers up to 10 MVA and 33 kV, with a new greenfield transformer plant in Ambala under planning) acquired in April 2026; incorporation of Saatvik Power Storage Solutions Limited in March 2026 for battery energy storage, with the Group evaluating storage opportunities of up to 20 GW over five years; and a 49% stake with management control in Intelligent Hydel Solutions Private Limited, which holds a PPA with MSEDCL for a 41 MW AC solar project.

outlook.body:
- Sustained domestic solar demand: India added a record 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26 (87% YoY growth) and total installed solar capacity crossed 150 GW by March 2026
- Policy support for domestic manufacturing: ALMM List-I for modules, ALMM List-II for cells mandatory from June 01, 2026, and ALMM List-III extending to wafers from 1 June 2028
- Tariff protection through the BCD and AIDC regime (40% on modules, 25% on cells plus AIDC surcharges) shielding domestic manufacturers from Chinese dumping
- Government demand programmes: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana targeting 25-30 GW of residential rooftop over three years, PM-KUSUM agricultural solarisation, CPSU Scheme Phase-II targeting 12 GW with DCR modules, Solar Park Scheme and Green Open Access rules
- Rising Renewable Consumption Obligation targets for obligated entities through FY 2029-30 supporting sustained module demand
- Mandatory energy storage in recent renewable bidding guidelines, expected to accelerate BESS deployment
- Margin lever from backward integration: the upcoming Odisha cell capacity is expected to materially reduce dependency on imported cells, currently the primary cost input, and improve gross margins
- Operating leverage from assets not yet in commercial production: management notes a meaningful share of capital is deployed in manufacturing assets yet to commence production, and expects commissioning and rising utilisation to improve operating leverage and support stronger profitability over time
- Margin headwind flagged during the year from industry-wide pricing normalisation, elevated solar cell procurement costs, and higher operating expenses associated with capacity expansion
- Sustained demand for high-efficiency n-Type TOPCon modules, with early adoption of Mono PERC and n-Type TOPCon supporting response to evolving efficiency and reliability requirements
- Structural competition backdrop: India's module manufacturing capacity expanded to over 120 GW by March 2026 from around 38 GW in March 2024, while cell capacity reached approximately 27 GW
- India's National Electricity Plan targets 609 GW of total installed capacity by FY2032 with solar projected at 364.6 GW, and the Government targets 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by FY 2030
- As on March 31, 2026, the confirmed order book stood at approximately 5.89 GW, providing strong revenue visibility for the coming quarters
- The order book comprises a balanced mix of utility-scale, commercial & industrial, and government projects, supporting business stability while mitigating customer concentration risk
- A diversified customer base and strong market presence enabled healthy order inflows through FY 2025-26, with robust demand across utility-scale, C&I and government-led solar projects
- EPC track record of 500 MW+ projects executed and 21+ marquee projects completed

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Saatvik Green Energy is an Indian renewable energy equipment manufacturer and turnkey solar solutions provider operating 4.8 GW of annual solar module capacity at Ambala, Haryana while building an integrated clean-energy platform.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Incorporated in 2015 and listed on the NSE and BSE in September 2025, Saatvik manufactures high-efficiency solar PV modules (Mono PERC and n-Type TOPCon, in mono-facial and bifacial configurations) and executes end-to-end solar EPC projects, supported by Operations & Maintenance services. It is integrating upstream into EPE encapsulant film, solar cells and planned ingots and wafers, and downstream into power electronics, transformers and battery energy storage. Customers span utility-scale, commercial & industrial, residential rooftop, agricultural and distributed energy applications across India and export markets.

- Sustained domestic solar demand: India added a record 44.6 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26 (87% YoY growth) and total installed solar capacity crossed 150 GW by March 2026

- Mandatory energy storage in recent renewable bidding guidelines, expected to accelerate BESS deployment
- Margin lever from backward integration: the upcoming Odisha cell capacity is expected to materially reduce dependency on imported cells, currently the primary cost input, and improve gross margins
- Operating leverage from assets not yet in commercial production: management notes a meaningful share of capital is deployed in manufacturing assets yet to commence production, and expects commissioning and rising utilisation to improve operating leverage and support stronger profitability over time

- Sustained demand for high-efficiency n-Type TOPCon modules, with early adoption of Mono PERC and n-Type TOPCon supporting response to evolving efficiency and reliability requirements
- Structural competition backdrop: India's module manufacturing capacity expanded to over 120 GW by March 2026 from around 38 GW in March 2024, while cell capacity reached approximately 27 GW

capex_expansion.body: Saatvik is executing a phased capacity expansion built around backward integration. The flagship Odisha Greenfield Integrated Manufacturing Project at Gopalpur, spearheaded by wholly owned subsidiary Saatvik Solar Industries Private Limited, saw civil and structural works across the solar cells and modules units substantially completed during FY 2025-26. Phase I comprises 2.4 GW of solar cell capacity and 4 GW of module capacity, both under ramp-up, with the ALMM-II inspection planned for September 2026; Phase II is planned to add a further 3.6 GW of solar cells, taking planned Odisha cell capacity to 6 GW (raised during the year from 4.8 GW). A further 6 GW of ingot and wafer capacity is planned, with commissioning targeted by FY29. On completion, total module manufacturing capacity is expected to rise from 4.8 GW at Ambala to 8.8 GW across Haryana and Odisha. At Ambala the Company commissioned a 2 GW EPE encapsulant film facility during the year and plans to enhance encapsulant capacity to 5 GW across Ambala and Odisha (Odisha encapsulant of 2 GW is planned). Management plans to invest approximately INR 17,000 million in FY 2026-27, primarily in the Odisha project, funded through a balanced mix of internal accruals and debt while remaining within the targeted gearing range; approximately 56% of IPO proceeds had been deployed towards manufacturing expansion, backward integration and debt reduction as of March 31, 2026. - Inverters: assembly manufacturing being set up. Solar pumps: standalone BU. Storage: flagged in closing remarks (nascent).
- Ingot/wafer: working on it, plans "ready"; will firm up after draft policy clarity (policy targeted ~June 2028). US export: <1% now, will re-pursue post tariff cut to 18% from 50% (over-and-above Section 201 ~14% — still being evaluated).
margins & cost dynamics:
- Margin lever = backward integration: cells + DCR + in-house encapsulant. Silver is the swing input (now ~25% of module cost).
- Pass-through is partial: protected on long-term orders, exposed on short-term/spot. Govt budget exemption on glass raw material could ease module input costs over 1-2 yrs (Saatvik not in glass mfg itself).
capex / expansion:
- Odisha integrated project: 4 GW module (commission ~Mar 2026, commercial Q1FY27) + 4.8 GW cell (commission Jul-Sep 2026, commercial ~Oct 2026). Module capacity 4.8 → 8.8 GW in FY27 (ramped, not full-year).
- Total capex INR 1,850 cr (cell portion ~INR 1,350 cr); fully funded (equity + debt raised); deployed by H2FY27. Ground-breaking to cell commercial ≈ 15-18 months.
capital allocation: - Net debt INR 749 cr (incl. term + working capital) at end-9MFY26. Leverage temporarily up from inventory pre-securing; mgmt stresses "capital discipline" and "disciplined growth over aggressive volume." No dividend/buyback discussion.
risks & watch-items:
- Commodity volatility (silver ~9% daily swings) compressing spot-order margins.
- Industry overcapacity: ~140 GW ALMM module capacity, cell capacity 26 GW (12 GW obsolete Mono PERC) heading to 50-60 GW — mgmt downplays (industry util only 40-50%).
- Execution risk on Odisha cell ramp/efficiency stabilization. Rising interest cost. US tariff/policy uncertainty (final terms unsigned). Demand timing tied to ALMM cell mandate (tenders from ~June 2026, 18-24 month lag to installation).
management quality / tone: - Confident, execution-focused; candid on margin dip drivers and partial pass-through; refused to disclose absolute realizations/market prices (typical). Emphasized 10-yr track record and disciplined growth. Some defensiveness/circularity in the flat-volume QoQ exchange. Credible on funding (fully tied up).
non-obvious takeaways:
- The real margin re-rating is cell/DCR-led from H2FY27, not module volume — module pricing is a commodity pass-through game.
- Interest-cost spike is a deliberate strategic inventory bet on rising cell/silver prices, not distress — watch if it actually normalizes by March.
- Q4→Q1FY27 volume explicitly flagged flattish; new 4 GW module won't be fully available in FY27 (ramp). Mono PERC obsolescence is a tailwind for new cell capacity vs incumbents.
- Solar pump BU and inverter assembly are early call-options, immaterial today.

themes.title: Solar PV cell-to-module manufacturing
themes.need: Solar module/cell manufacturers ride capacity ramp, ALMM/DCR protection and an order-book build-out - a manufacturing thesis distinct from firm-power/FDRE tender economics or merchant storage arbitrage. Q1FY27 quantified the DCR arbitrage: EMMVEE grew revenue 51% to INR 1,555cr with EBITDA margin up to 35.2% and PAT +103% on a 9.9 GW order book, with DCR modules earning INR 8.5-9/W of EBITDA against INR 2-2.5/W for non-DCR - a 3-4x per-watt gap that structurally separates integrated cell makers from module assemblers. The offset is order timing: SWSOLAR booked a record INR 13,000cr unexecuted order value on a landmark USD 560m Egypt win (1,000 MW solar + 600 MWh BESS) yet revenue still fell 10% YoY, and flagged that industry orders concluded only ~INR 6,400cr against the >INR 20,000cr expected, deferred by DCR/module-price uncertainty.
themes.driver: DCR cell/module capacity commissioning and the ALMM List-2 per-watt spread; domestic ordering restarting after two slow quarters (SWSOLAR); order-book conversion.
